description_good_justification: The README opens by saying what ReviewDesk is for, in plain words: free software for running the record-handling stages of a systematic review as a team (logging searches, importing and de-duplicating records, screening, full-text review, data extraction, risk of bias, GRADE and the PRISMA 2020 outputs). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/README.md
interact_justification: The README says how to obtain ReviewDesk ("Download and start": the Releases page), how to give feedback ("Status and support": open an issue) and how to contribute (CONTRIBUTING.md). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/README.md
contribution_justification: CONTRIBUTING.md, "Sending a change": changes come in as GitHub pull requests to main (fork, branch, tests, pull request), and anything larger than a small fix starts as an issue. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
contribution_requirements_justification: CONTRIBUTING.md ("Code", "Running the tests", "Static analysis") and docs/dev/DESIGN.md ("Rules that every change must keep") give the requirements: Python standard library only, Python 3.9 or later, who may write which file, blinding, the wording of the pages, a test for every change, and tests and static analysis that pass. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/docs/dev/DESIGN.md
floss_license_osi_justification: The MIT License is approved by the Open Source Initiative.
license_location_justification: LICENSE, at the top of the repository; NOTICE.txt beside it lists the third-party parts of the downloads and their licences. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/LICENSE
documentation_basics_justification: The README says how to get, start and upgrade ReviewDesk and what it sends where; the user guide (PDF and Word) covers every stage of use, with sections on working safely in a shared folder and on what is stored where; a set-up walk-through takes a project lead through a first review; SECURITY.md says what ReviewDesk protects against and what it does not. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/README.md https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/docs/ReviewDesk%20user%20guide.pdf https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/SECURITY.md
documentation_interface_justification: ReviewDesk is an application used through its pages, and files go in and come out. The user guide describes every page; the README names the export formats it reads (RIS, PubMed .nbib, Cochrane, Web of Science, CSV) and sections 5, 6 and 13 of the user guide say how to export, import and what each output is; the reporting pack's "Read me first" file and the read-me in the evaluation data describe every file written (the latter column by column). docs/dev/DESIGN.md ("Starting ReviewDesk: options and settings") documents the command-line options and environment variables. The requests between its pages and its local server are internal, not an interface for other programs. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/docs/ReviewDesk%20user%20guide.pdf https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/docs/dev/DESIGN.md
sites_https_justification: The repository, its issues and its downloads are on github.com, over HTTPS only. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk
english_justification: All documentation is in English, and reports and comments are taken in English.
maintained_justification: ReviewDesk is maintained by its author; the README ("Status and support") says what to expect, and that anything that could lose work or give a wrong result comes first. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/README.md
repo_public_justification: The repository is public on GitHub. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk
repo_track_justification: Git, on GitHub: every change with its author and date.
repo_interim_justification: From version 1.3.1 on, development is done in the open: every change is an ordinary public commit or pull request on the main branch, visible before the release that contains it. The repository was first published at 1.3.1 as a single commit, so the history of earlier versions is not in it. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/commits/main
version_unique_justification: Every release has its own version number (for example 1.3.1): in `app/reviewdesk/__init__.py`, CITATION.cff, the change log, the names of the downloads and at the bottom of the program's menu. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md
version_semver_justification: Versions are major.minor.patch, as in Semantic Versioning.
version_tags_justification: From 1.3.1, the first public version, each release is a git tag (v1.3.1) with a GitHub Release. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/releases
release_notes_justification: CHANGELOG.md has an entry written for people for every version, and each GitHub Release carries notes that say what the version is and how to upgrade (UPGRADING.md). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/releases
release_notes_vulns_justification: No vulnerability in ReviewDesk has been publicly known. SECURITY.md says that a security fix is named as one in the change log and the release notes. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/SECURITY.md
report_process_justification: GitHub issues, with a template that asks for the version, the system and the steps; the README and CONTRIBUTING.md say how. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/issues
report_responses_justification: Reports are answered by the maintainer in the issue tracker. ReviewDesk became public with version 1.3.1 in November 2026, and no report had been received when this was written. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/issues?q=is%3Aissue
enhancement_responses_justification: Requests are answered by the maintainer in the issue tracker; none had been received when this was written (ReviewDesk became public in November 2026). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/issues?q=is%3Aissue
report_archive_justification: GitHub keeps every issue and its answers, open or closed, and they can be searched. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/issues?q=is%3Aissue
vulnerability_report_private_justificati: GitHub's private vulnerability reporting is switched on: "Report a vulnerability" on the repository's "Security and quality" tab, as SECURITY.md says. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/security/advisories/new
vulnerability_report_response_justificat: No vulnerability report has been received.
build_justification: Nothing is compiled: ReviewDesk is Python and plain JavaScript and runs from its source as it is. (tools/build_release.py only packs the files into the download zips, reproducibly.)
build_floss_tools_justification: Nothing is compiled; see "build". The script that packs the downloads needs only Python and git.
test_justification: A pytest suite of over a thousand tests in tests/, under the same MIT License. CONTRIBUTING.md ("Running the tests") says how to run it (python3 -m pytest), and .github/workflows/tests.yml runs it on GitHub. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
test_invocation_justification: python3 -m pytest, from the top of the repository (pytest.ini): the usual way for Python.
test_most_justification: The suite runs 92% of the lines and 85% of the branches of ReviewDesk's Python (coverage.py, version 1.3.1 on Linux, the ReviewDesk programs that the tests start included; CONTRIBUTING.md, "Coverage", says how to measure it), and opens every page in Chromium. The code that only Windows runs, such as the encryption of the saved key, is tested on Windows. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
test_continuous_integration_justificatio: GitHub Actions runs the suite on every push and pull request, on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS with the oldest and the newest Python supported, and once more with the browser tests. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/actions
test_policy_justification: CONTRIBUTING.md ("Add tests for what you change") and docs/dev/DESIGN.md ("Add a test for everything you change, and run the whole suite before you send it"). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
tests_are_added_justification: What was new in 1.3.1 is tested: the verification sample, time recording and the evaluation data in tests/test_evaluation.py and tests/test_evaluation_ui.py, the whole fingerprints in tests/test_fingerprints.py, and the Windows fix in tests/test_security.py. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/tree/main/tests
tests_documented_added_justification: CONTRIBUTING.md, and the pull-request form has a box for it ("What is new or changed has a test"). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/.github/pull_request_template.md
warnings_justification: Ruff reads the Python (pyflakes, flake8-bugbear, pylint's error rules and flake8-bandit: ruff.toml) and ESLint the JavaScript (its recommended rules, eslint-plugin-no-unsanitized, and no-eval and its relatives: eslint.config.mjs). The JavaScript is all ES modules, which are always in strict mode. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/ruff.toml https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/eslint.config.mjs
warnings_fixed_justification: Both report nothing on the released code, and the "static analysis" workflow fails on any finding. The few lines where a tool is wrong say so on the line, with the reason; each rule switched off for the whole project has its reason beside it in ruff.toml.
warnings_strict_justification: Ruff's pyflakes, bugbear, pylint-error and bandit rule sets are on for the program, apart from four rules switched off for the whole project and a few more for one file, the developer tools and the tests, each with its reason beside it in ruff.toml; ESLint's recommended rules, no-unsanitized, and no-eval and its relatives are on for the pages. Every finding is an error that fails the workflow. Rules about style are not used. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/ruff.toml
know_secure_design_justification: The project's developer knows these principles and designed ReviewDesk by them; SECURITY.md and docs/dev/DESIGN.md set out how each is applied. Economy of mechanism: Python's standard library only, with no database, no accounts and no server on the internet. Fail-safe defaults: a request is refused unless it carries the session token and comes from ReviewDesk's own page, and the AI screener, time recording and the verification sample are off until the project lead switches them on. Complete mediation: every request passes the same checks before any of the program's own code for it runs, and roles and blinding are checked on the server, not only hidden on the page. Open design: the code is public, and only keys are secret. Separation of privilege: a request needs the session token and must also come from ReviewDesk's own page, addressed to this computer. Least privilege: it runs as the ordinary user, listens on this computer only, its pages may load only its own files, and the AI key goes only to the address it was saved with. Least common mechanism: each person's work is in files of their own, and there is no shared server. Psychological acceptability: no passwords to manage, and the safe choice is the default. Limited attack surface: one local address, no third-party packages, pages that load nothing from the internet, and two optional features that send anything out. Input validation with allowlists: every request that changes something must match its declared shape (app/reviewdesk/shapes.py). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/SECURITY.md https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/docs/dev/DESIGN.md
know_common_errors_justification: The developer knows the common errors in a local web application of this kind, and ReviewDesk counters each (SECURITY.md lists them, and the tests check each one). Cross-site scripting: text from records goes on the page as text, the one place that sets markup escapes every piece, and the browser is told to run no inline script. Requests forged by another site, and DNS rebinding: the session token, and a check of the Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site and Host of every request. Path traversal: files are named by ReviewDesk, never by a request. Server-side request forgery: the PDF finder follows only addresses on the public internet, checked when looked up, after every redirect and on connection. Injection: there is no database, and no command is built from data. Leaked secrets: the AI key never reaches the browser or the shared folder, is not sent after a redirect, and is removed from logged errors. Oversized input: a request body over the limit is refused. Static analysis looks for these on every push (.github/workflows/analysis.yml). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/SECURITY.md
crypto_published_justification: SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-256 (Python's hashlib and hmac), kept whole, for the data checks; TLS, as Python's ssl module provides it, for every https connection (always for the AI service, unless it is on the same computer, and for the open-access search services; a PDF is then fetched from whatever public web address they give); and, on Windows, the operating system's Data Protection API to keep the saved AI key encrypted.
crypto_call_justification: ReviewDesk implements no cryptography itself: it calls Python's standard library (hashlib, hmac, secrets, ssl) and, on Windows, the operating system's Data Protection API.
crypto_floss_justification: Everything cryptographic is done by Python's standard library (with OpenSSL underneath), which is FLOSS. On Windows the saved AI key is also encrypted with the operating system's own Data Protection API; on Mac and Linux it is kept in a file that only the user's account can read.
crypto_keylength_justification: Hashes: every fingerprint the data checks keep (of each row of decisions, each screened record, the review question and criteria, each export and each PDF) is a whole SHA-256, and every row signature a whole HMAC-SHA-256: 256 bits. Keys: each computer's signing secret is 128 random bits, and the session token 192 random bits. TLS uses Python's default settings, which from Python 3.10 refuse keys weaker than 112 bits (OpenSSL security level 2); the Windows download carries Python 3.14, and with Python 3.9, the oldest supported, the level is that of the computer's own OpenSSL. Shorter cannot be chosen: there is no setting for it, and in a project begun with 1.3.1 or later a fingerprint or signature shorter than the whole is refused. Versions before 1.3.1 kept only the first 80 or 64 bits; what they wrote stays in the projects of that time, where it is checked as it was, and everything added since is whole (the notes at the top of app/reviewdesk/integrity.py give the rules, and tests/test_fingerprints.py holds them). The start of a SHA-256 is still used to name things (a project, a prompt, a problem in the data checks, the text an AI answer was given for): those are names to look things up by, not what the data checks rely on. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/app/reviewdesk/integrity.py
crypto_working_justification: No MD5, SHA-1, DES or RC4 anywhere: only SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-256, and TLS with Python's default settings, which check the server's certificate.
crypto_weaknesses_justification: As for "crypto_working": nothing with a known serious weakness is used.
crypto_pfs_justification: ReviewDesk has no key agreement of its own. Its only encrypted connections are the HTTPS requests it makes, with Python's default TLS settings: from Python 3.10 (the Windows download carries 3.14) these offer only forward-secret key exchange, and TLS 1.3 always uses it. With Python 3.9, the oldest supported, a server that speaks only TLS 1.2 could still choose a key exchange that is not forward-secret.
crypto_password_storage_justification: ReviewDesk has no accounts and stores no passwords for signing in. (The key for the AI service, which it has to send out, is covered under "crypto_floss".)
crypto_random_justification: The session token and each computer's signing secret come from Python's secrets module. Python's random module is used only where a result has to be repeatable from a recorded seed (drawing and shuffling screening samples, the resamples behind a confidence interval) and to space out retries: never for a secret (ruff.toml records this beside rule S311). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/ruff.toml
delivery_mitm_justification: The downloads are GitHub Releases, over HTTPS, and the release notes give each zip's SHA-256. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/releases
delivery_unsigned_justification: The checksums are on the HTTPS release page beside the downloads. When a release is built, the Python for the Windows download is fetched from python.org over HTTPS and refused unless it matches a SHA-256 written in tools/build_release.py.
vulnerabilities_fixed_60_days_justificat: There is no publicly known vulnerability in ReviewDesk.
vulnerabilities_critical_fixed_justifica: None has been reported. SECURITY.md says how to report one privately and that a fix comes out as a new version. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/SECURITY.md
no_leaked_credentials_justification: The repository holds no credentials. The tests use invented keys against a stand-in service on the same computer, and the public repository was started from one commit of the release, so it has no earlier history. GitHub's secret scanning and push protection are on.
static_analysis_justification: Every push and pull request is analysed by .github/workflows/analysis.yml: Ruff (with the flake8-bugbear and flake8-bandit rules) for the Python, ESLint with eslint-plugin-no-unsanitized for the JavaScript, and CodeQL with its security-extended queries for both, which is also scheduled weekly. Before 1.3.1 was released the code was also read with Bandit and with Semgrep's community rules for Python, JavaScript, HTML and secrets. https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/.github/workflows/analysis.yml
static_analysis_common_vulnerabilities_j: CodeQL's security-extended queries, Ruff's bandit rules and ESLint's no-unsanitized rules exist to find common vulnerabilities: injection, cross-site scripting, unsafe requests and file paths, weak cryptography.
static_analysis_fixed_justification: No vulnerability found by static analysis is open. A finding fails the workflow (Ruff, ESLint) or is a code scanning alert (CodeQL), and every one is fixed, or dismissed with its reason, before a release is built (docs/dev/RELEASING.md). https://github.com/cphumphries/ReviewDesk/blob/main/docs/dev/RELEASING.md
static_analysis_often_justification: On every push and pull request; CodeQL is also scheduled weekly, while the repository is active.
dynamic_analysis_justification: The automated test suite is run on every push and before every release, and runs 85% of the branches of ReviewDesk's Python (see "test_most"), which is above the 80% this criterion asks of a test suite. No fuzzer or web application scanner is used.
dynamic_analysis_unsafe_justification: ReviewDesk is Python and JavaScript: there is no memory-unsafe language in it.
dynamic_analysis_enable_assertions_justi: ReviewDesk's own code has no assert statements to switch on. Its run-time checks (the shape of every request that changes something, the chained fingerprints of every row of decisions) are ordinary code that always runs, in the tests and in use.
dynamic_analysis_fixed_justification: Running the tests, which is the dynamic analysis used, has found no vulnerability, so none is open.
